interactions.summary: A student reads Beatrice's warning not to make vows rashly, using Jephthah as the example of someone who should have admitted error instead of keeping faith in a disastrous vow.
Jiang retells the Jephthah story, presses the class to judge it non-relativistically, and insists that Beatrice's point is stark: Jephthah should have broken the vow rather than kill his daughter.

A student tries to resolve the paradox by linking Piccarda's imperfect vow and Jephthah's impossible promise, and Jiang keeps pressing until another student argues that taking vows seriously means understanding their weight and not making them rashly in the first place.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reasoning under Jiang's paradox prompt

claims.claim: The quoted Dante passage says mortals should never take vows rashly, and that Jephthah should have said 'I did amiss' rather than commit a worse act by keeping faith with a bad vow.
Jiang recounts Jephthah's vow as a promise to offer the first person through his door if God grants victory, which results in his daughter becoming the fatal object of the vow.
Jiang interprets Beatrice as saying Jephthah should have broken the vow rather than fulfill it through murder, so vow-keeping is not an absolute good when the vow itself is corrupt.
The student resolution Jiang accepts is that taking vows seriously includes understanding their weight before making them and refusing rash vows rather than blindly honoring any promise once spoken.
claims.temporal_scope: Student formulation accepted as useful on 2026-06-16.

signature_moments.moment: The packet's governing reversal is already in the quoted line: better to confess 'I did amiss' than to do something worse in the name of fidelity.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Dante's moral inversion of simplistic vow-keeping and anchors the whole paradox Jiang is building.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes the point brutally plain: if keeping a vow means killing your daughter, then break the vow.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest ethical compression and will likely matter in the public read because it keeps the lecture from sounding abstractly scholastic.

signature_moments.moment: The paradox Jiang forces on the class is that Jephthah took his vows seriously in exactly the wrong way, so seriousness must include judgment before and within the vow.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses the distinction between fidelity and discernment that the later discussion on forgiveness and self-command keeps worrying.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The biblical judge whose disastrous vow becomes Beatrice's example of why rash promise-making cannot be redeemed by literal fulfillment alone.
A promise made without circumspection, whose later fulfillment can become morally worse than its breach.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet sharpens the prior Arendt-style praise of promise-making by immediately testing it against Dante's Jephthah paradox: promise and fidelity are still real goods, but they are not permission to suspend judgment about evil means.
